It is built for work and not personal errands. Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, introduced an A.I. agent on Wednesday that acts as a personal digital assistant. Called Claude Duet, the tool is in an early test phase but joins a fast-growing field of A.I. assistants that take actions and perform tasks on their own. It will compete with OpenAI’s dots, which debuted last month; Meta’s Muse; Google’s Gemini Spark; and agents from the start-up Instinct, which raised $1 billion in its latest funding round. Unlike OpenAI and Meta, which have pitched their agents as assistants for everyday tasks like booking reservations, Anthropic said Claude Duet was built for work and was less capable at personal errands. Claude Duet is Anthropic’s most direct attempt to move its chatbot from answering questions to running parts of people’s working lives.

OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC. Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials. OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors.

They showed it could invent, build and maintain technology better than the same number of agents working alone. The study ran on a hosted frontier model. A research team working with Apex Fusion has now reproduced the central experiment on four RTX 3090 gaming GPUs. Apex Fusion is a Swiss foundation building infrastructure for AI agents. The MIT team released its code, prompts and complete traces, which is what made an outside replication possible. The replication, led by Časlav Nedeljković of HAL8, set out to test whether SwarmWorld’s result depended on a frontier model. The replication itself ran directly on the team’s own GPUs. The team also registered its model server as a supplier on the Vector marketplace, an OpenAI-compatible gateway that meters each request and settles usage on-chain in AP3X, the network’s utility token.

highlights: Nvidia has released a design for running AI agents inside fixed limits, from enterprise infrastructure to edge machines. Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta, Microsoft, Google Cloud and AWS are among the companies working with it, Nvidia said. The design builds on OpenShell, Nvidia’s open source runtime software, which sets a boundary around what an agent can do. OpenShell is also part of the agent safety platform Nvidia launched in September. The software that drives the agents and their tools runs on Vera CPUs. BlueField-4 data processing units run Nvidia Sentry, software that watches agent behaviour from outside the main system. If an agent tries to move outside its software boundary, Sentry quarantines and stops it in milliseconds, Nvidia said. Agents from Anthropic, Cohere, Google, Meta, OpenAI, Perplexity, Reflection and SpaceX Super Intelligence can run on OpenShell infrastructure, Nvidia said. > “With the OpenShell Reference Architecture, agents can think on Rubin, act on Vera and be governed on BlueField,” Huang said.
